items.definition: an important stage or event that marks progress in a project
exampleSentences: The team celebrated reaching the project's first milestone.
Each milestone had its own deadline on the timeline.
Missing an early milestone can delay the whole project.

items.definition: the latest time or date by which something must be finished
exampleSentences: The design team missed the deadline by two days.
She works well under tight deadlines.
They moved the deadline forward by a week.

items.definition: a plan that shows when each part of a project should happen
exampleSentences: The project timeline was updated after the delay.
They stuck closely to the original timeline.
A realistic timeline prevents last-minute stress.

items.definition: something that must be produced or completed as part of a project
exampleSentences: The first deliverable is a working prototype.
Clients expect each deliverable on time.
The team split the deliverables among three people.

items.definition: a person or group with an interest in how a project turns out
exampleSentences: Every stakeholder reviewed the plan before it started.
The manager updates stakeholders every week.
Stakeholders raised concerns about the new timeline.

items.definition: the range of tasks and goals that a project is meant to cover
exampleSentences: The client wanted to expand the project's scope.
A clear scope keeps the team focused.
Adding new features widened the scope halfway through.

items.definition: a piece of work that someone must do as part of a larger job
exampleSentences: She finished her tasks ahead of schedule.
Each task on the list has its own deadline.
He was assigned a simple but time-consuming task.

items.definition: something such as time, money, or people that is available to complete a project
exampleSentences: The team lacked the resources to finish on time.
Extra resources were brought in to speed up the project.
They allocated resources carefully across departments.

items.definition: the series of steps that work passes through from start to finish
exampleSentences: The new software simplified the team's workflow.
A messy workflow led to repeated mistakes.
They redesigned the workflow to remove extra steps.

items.definition: a point in a process that slows everything down
exampleSentences: Approval from head office became a major bottleneck.
They identified the bottleneck and fixed it quickly.
Slow feedback created a bottleneck in the design process.

items.definition: to give part of your work or responsibility to someone else
exampleSentences: A good project manager knows how to delegate tasks.
She delegated the research to two team members.
He delegates small decisions so he can focus on strategy.

items.definition: to decide which tasks are most important and deal with them first
exampleSentences: The team had to prioritize the urgent bug fixes.
She prioritizes tasks by deadline every morning.
They prioritized customer-facing features over minor updates.

items.definition: to work together with other people to achieve something
exampleSentences: The two teams collaborated closely on the new app.
Designers and engineers collaborate throughout the project.
They collaborated remotely across three time zones.

items.definition: a person who works with you as part of the same team
exampleSentences: She asked a teammate to review her work.
Good teammates communicate openly about problems.
He covered for a teammate who was on leave.

items.definition: the person responsible for planning and organizing a project
exampleSentences: The project manager assigned tasks to each team member.
As project manager, she tracked every deliverable closely.
The new project manager reorganized the whole timeline.

items.definition: a plan that you prepare in advance so that you know what to do if something goes wrong
exampleSentences: We need a contingency plan in case the supplier delivers late.
When the server failed, the team switched to its contingency plan.
Every major project should have a contingency plan for key risks.
collocations: put a contingency plan in place

items.definition: later than planned, so that work is not finished at the time it should be
exampleSentences: The building work is three weeks behind schedule.
Bad weather put the delivery behind schedule.
If testing falls further behind schedule, we will miss the launch date.

items.definition: to introduce something new, such as a system or product, gradually across an organization
exampleSentences: The company plans to roll out the new system next month.
They rolled out the update to a small group first.
The team is rolling out the changes region by region.

items.definition: a short document that describes how much work has been completed so far
exampleSentences: She sends a progress report to the client every Friday.
The progress report showed the project was on track.
He included risks in his weekly progress report.

items.definition: making the expected progress, so that something is likely to be finished on time or succeed
exampleSentences: Despite the delay in July, the project is still on track for a March launch.
Weekly check-ins help keep everyone on track.
The manager asked what extra support we needed to get back on track.

items.definition: a move to a higher position or rank at work
exampleSentences: She earned a promotion after leading the successful project.
His promotion came with more responsibility.
They celebrated his promotion to senior manager.

items.definition: the sequence of jobs and experiences a person follows over their working life
exampleSentences: Her career path took her from intern to director.
He wasn't sure which career path to follow after graduation.
Mentors can help you plan a realistic career path.

items.definition: to formally leave a job or position
exampleSentences: She decided to resign after ten years at the company.
He resigned from his position last spring.
Two engineers resigned within the same month.

items.definition: an official record showing that someone has finished training or passed an exam
exampleSentences: The job requires a specific qualification in engineering.
She listed her qualifications at the top of her resume.
Extra qualifications helped him stand out among applicants.

items.definition: a period of supervised work experience, often for students or new graduates
exampleSentences: She completed a summer internship at a design firm.
His internship turned into a full-time job offer.
The internship gave her real experience in project work.

items.definition: an experienced person who advises and guides someone with less experience
exampleSentences: Her mentor helped her prepare for the promotion.
New employees are paired with a mentor in their first month.
He still calls his old mentor for advice.

items.definition: the particular abilities and knowledge that a person has for a job
exampleSentences: The role requires a broad skill set in design and coding.
She expanded her skill set by taking online courses.
His technical skill set made him perfect for the project.

items.definition: a formal proposal from a company inviting someone to work for them
exampleSentences: She accepted a job offer from a larger company.
He turned down the job offer to stay with his current team.
The job offer included a higher salary and more flexibility.

items.definition: a person who formally asks to be considered for a job, a place on a course, or something similar
exampleSentences: The advertisement for a project manager attracted more than two hundred applicants.
Only three applicants were invited to a second interview.
The successful applicant will start in September.

items.definition: working independently for different clients rather than for one employer
exampleSentences: She left her office job to work as a freelance designer.
He freelances for several companies at once.
Freelance work gave her more control over her schedule.

lessons.title: Grammar: Future forms for plans and deadlines

items.headword: future forms for plans and deadlines
items.definition: how to talk about plans, arrangements and deadlines using will, going to, present continuous and the future perfect
items.explanationTR:
English uses different future forms depending on how fixed or certain a plan is.

• Present continuous for fixed arrangements: The designers are presenting the prototype on Thursday.
• "Going to" for intentions and evidence-based predictions: We're going to miss the deadline unless we get more help.
• Will for decisions made at the moment of speaking, offers and promises, and predictions based on opinion (often with I think or probably): I'll send the deliverable by Friday.
• Future perfect for an action completed before a future deadline: By June, she will have finished her internship.
• Future continuous for an action in progress at a specific future time: This time next week, the team will be rolling out the update.

Use "going to" when a plan or decision already exists, and "will" when you decide at the moment of speaking. Use the future perfect specifically to talk about deadlines: something that will already be done by a certain point in time. Often more than one form is possible, so choose the one that matches what you mean.

In project and career contexts, choosing the right future form makes timelines and commitments clear to teammates and clients.

questions.prompt: We ---- the new feature next Monday. It's already on the calendar.
questions.explanationTR: A fixed arrangement already on the calendar is naturally expressed with the present continuous (are launching); "launched," "have launched" and "were launching" refer to the past and clash with "next Monday," and "are going to launching" is not a grammatical form.

questions.prompt: Look at how much work is still left on the list. We ---- the deadline.
questions.explanationTR: A prediction based on present evidence (the work still left on the list) uses "going to" (are going to miss); "will have been missing" wrongly adds a continuous aspect to a simple prediction.

questions.prompt: You look really busy. Leave the slides to me — I ---- them tomorrow morning.
questions.explanationTR: An offer made at the moment of speaking uses "will" (I'll prepare / will prepare); "prepared" and "have prepared" refer to the past and clash with "tomorrow morning," and "would prepare" is a conditional form with no condition.

questions.prompt: By the end of the month, she ---- her internship.
questions.explanationTR: The future perfect (will have finished) shows an action completed before a stated future deadline ("by the end of the month"); "has finished," "finished" and "had finished" look back from the present or the past, not from a point in the future.

questions.prompt: This time next week, the whole team ---- on the new rollout.
questions.explanationTR: The future continuous (will be working) describes an action in progress at a specific future moment ("this time next week"); the simple future (will work) does not capture that ongoing sense.

questions.prompt:
A: Sam has just finished his own work for today.
B: Oh, good. In that case, I ---- the report to him.
questions.explanationTR: B decides at the moment of speaking, after hearing the news ("In that case"), so "will" is used (I'll delegate / will delegate); "delegated" and "have delegated" describe something already done, and "would delegate" needs a condition.

questions.prompt: It's confirmed: we ---- the prototype to the client at 10 a.m. tomorrow.
questions.explanationTR: A confirmed arrangement with a specific time ("10 a.m. tomorrow") is naturally expressed with the present continuous (are presenting); the past forms clash with "tomorrow," and "are going to presenting" is not a grammatical form.

questions.prompt: Please don't call Kenji between 2 and 4 p.m. tomorrow — he ---- the client workshop then.
questions.explanationTR: An action in progress during a specific future period ("between 2 and 4 p.m. tomorrow") uses the future continuous (will be running); "will have run" would mean the workshop is already over by then, and the other options refer to the past.

items.definition: An update email to a project team and seven questions about it

passage.title: A Project Update
passage.body:
Dear team,

Here is a short update on where the mobile app project stands. We are two weeks away from the final deadline, and most of the milestones on our timeline have already been reached. The design deliverable was approved last week, and the development team is now testing the last few features before the rollout.

There was one bottleneck in July, when the testing team had to wait for feedback from stakeholders before continuing. Once that feedback arrived, the workflow returned to normal, and we managed to catch up within a few days. To keep the project on track, our project manager decided to delegate two smaller tasks to team members with lighter workloads.

The scope of the project has stayed close to the original plan, with only minor changes to the settings screen. Everyone has worked hard, and the extra effort has not gone unnoticed. In fact, our project manager mentioned that Dana, who joined the team as an intern last year, will likely receive a promotion once the rollout is complete. Her mentor, Farah, says Dana's growing skill set made her the obvious choice.

Our next progress report will go out after the rollout, once we can share real results from users. Until then, please continue sending any concerns to your team lead so we can address them before the deadline.

Thank you all for your hard work this month.

Best,
Priya

questions.prompt: According to the update, how close is the team to the final deadline?
questions.explanationTR: Priya writes that the team is "two weeks away from the final deadline"; the other options do not match the timeframe stated in the update.

questions.prompt: What caused the bottleneck mentioned in the update?
options: A delay in feedback from stakeholders
A sudden change in project scope
A problem with the testing software
questions.explanationTR: The update says the team "had to wait for feedback from stakeholders before continuing"; the other causes are never mentioned as the source of the delay.

questions.prompt: What did the project manager do to keep the project on track after the bottleneck?
options: The scope of the project was reduced
Two tasks were delegated to team members with lighter workloads
A new, more experienced project manager was brought in to take over the schedule
The rollout was canceled for the month
questions.explanationTR: The update states the project manager "decided to delegate two smaller tasks to team members with lighter workloads"; the passage never mentions extending the deadline or hiring anyone new.

questions.prompt: What is expected to happen to Dana after the rollout?
options: She will resign from the company
She will take a probation period
She will likely receive a promotion
She will be given a smaller workload
questions.explanationTR: The update says Dana "will likely receive a promotion once the rollout is complete"; Farah is described as Dana's mentor, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Based on the update, when will the next progress report be sent?
options: Right when the bottleneck first appeared, before it was even resolved
As soon as the scope changed
At the very start of the project
After the rollout, once results from users are available
questions.explanationTR: Priya writes that the "next progress report will go out after the rollout, once we can share real results from users"; no fixed weekly schedule is mentioned in the update.

questions.prompt: How has the project's scope changed compared to the original plan?
options: It has stayed close to the original plan, with only minor changes
It expanded to include several new features
It was cut in half to save time
It changed completely once the stakeholders asked for a much larger set of features than planned
It was replaced by a completely different plan
questions.explanationTR: The update says the scope "has stayed close to the original plan, with only minor changes to the settings screen"; no major expansion or replacement is described.

questions.prompt: According to Farah, why is Dana the obvious choice for a promotion?
questions.explanationTR: The update says that Farah, Dana's mentor, believes "Dana's growing skill set made her the obvious choice"; Dana joined only last year as an intern, and workloads, reports and stakeholders are mentioned in other contexts.
